accuracy.evidence: Corner and side counts checked against Development Matters (3 and 4 year olds: talk about 2D shapes using 'sides', 'corners', 'straight', 'flat', 'round'): square 4 sides and 4 corners, triangle 3 and 3, rectangle 2 long and 2 short sides, circle and oval no corners. The fit rule in the lab is the real one: a piece drops in only at whole multiples of its rotational symmetry (circle any angle, square every quarter turn, triangle every third of a turn, rectangle every half turn), which the adult text states.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented toddler errors in shape sorting: pushing harder instead of rotating (prediction 1 and challenge 'Push harder'), offering a square to the rectangle hole because both have four corners ('The rectangle is too long for the square hole' and the reverse in the challenge), believing a turned triangle is a different shape, and thinking a circle has corners (prediction 3).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is a working shape sorter: a piece's angle is checked against the hole's symmetry, so a right shape at a wrong turn bumps back; tapping a held piece turns it 30 degrees; shapes are released on a slope where only the circle rolls with real spin; and a corners sort draws and counts the corners. None of this is a relabelled sorter or matcher; it passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child matches outlines first, then meets an upside-down triangle that will not drop until turned, then a standing rectangle that must lie flat, then sees the circle roll while the square slides and the triangle stays, then sorts by corners with the corners drawn and counted, then combines matching and turning in a full sorter. The text after each task only names what the child just did.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'Will the upside-down triangle go in? Yes, push hard' (it bumps back until turned), 'Which shape will roll? The square' (it slides and stops), and 'Does a circle have corners? Yes, 4' (it lands in No corners with no dots).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve distinct wrong-answer m= messages, each naming the slip: pushing instead of turning, the round hole has no corners, the square slides not rolls, 4 corners is a square not a triangle, the rectangle hole is longer than the square, the square hole is too short for the rectangle, and standing up is the wrong way round.

readability.evidence: Kid text is short read-aloud sentences with concrete words (round, pointy, slope, plop) and stays under the family FK limit of 5.0; adult text stays under 10.0. Canvas prompts are four to six words, and the shape buttons use one shape word with a symbol (● Circle, ▲ Triangle).

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplication gate. Each kid paragraph does one job (match, turn, corners, roll); the adult text covers the skill, how toddlers progress from trial and error, named mistakes with symmetry, and what the lab does; the family tip is one homemade sorter plus a roll game.

mobile.evidence: On the iPhone 13 walkthrough and 360 px screenshots the sorter, holes and tray scale with the canvas width, holes keep a gap even with the rectangle beside the triangle, the young class gives 56 px buttons, and no more than six buttons show at once because a picked shape swaps the shape list for Turn, the free holes and Another.

accessibility.evidence: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and phone in the walkthrough. Every drag has a button route (pick a shape, Turn, then a named hole; Let go on the slope; Corners or No corners), and the canvas aria-label reports what is in the box, what is still out and whether a piece lines up.
